resources.title: Graphs and representations
resources.text:
# Synthetic notes: graphs and representations
A graph G=(V,E) contains vertices V and edges E. In a simple undirected graph,
an edge joins two different vertices and has no direction. The degree of a
vertex is the number of incident edges. Each edge contributes two to the sum
of all degrees, so sum(deg(v))=2|E|. Six edges give a degree sum of twelve.
An adjacency list stores the neighbors of each vertex. It uses O(V+E) memory.
Testing an edge may scan O(deg(v)) neighbors. An adjacency matrix uses O(V²)
memory and supports O(1) edge lookup. A sparse graph has far fewer edges than
V², so adjacency lists usually save memory. These are generated teaching notes,
not a TUM lecture or official exam.

For the three-vertex path A–B–C, the adjacency matrix is [[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]]. Squaring it gives [[1,0,1],[0,2,0],[1,0,1]]. The squared entry counts walks of exactly two edges, allowing repeated vertices.

resources.title: Breadth-first search
resources.text:
# Synthetic notes: breadth-first search
BFS uses a first-in, first-out queue. Mark a vertex as seen when it is enqueued.
Pop a vertex, inspect its neighbors, and enqueue only neighbors not yet seen.
BFS reaches vertices in nondecreasing distance from the start. In an unweighted
graph, the first discovery of v from u gives d(v)=d(u)+1. This is a shortest path
in number of edges, not in arbitrary total weight. An adjacency-list traversal
uses O(V+E) time and O(V) auxiliary memory. Consider an undirected graph with
edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-E, D-F, E-F. Inspect neighbors alphabetically. Starting at
A, expansion order is A,B,C,D,E,F. After expanding B the queue is C,D. The
shortest distance to F is three edges. When E sees F, F is already seen and is
not enqueued again. Dijkstra instead uses a minimum-priority queue and supports
nonnegative edge weights. DFS uses depth-first backtracking, not FIFO order.
These notes are synthetic.

resources.title: Depth-first search
resources.text:
# Synthetic notes: depth-first search
DFS follows one branch until no unseen neighbor remains, then backtracks to an
earlier vertex with remaining work. It uses recursion or an explicit stack.
Mark vertices as seen so cycles do not cause repeated traversal. An adjacency
list permits O(V+E) time. DFS does not guarantee a shortest path. On the sample
undirected graph A-B, A-C, B-D, C-E, D-F, E-F, an alphabetical recursive DFS
starting at A can discover C along A,B,D,F,E,C. That tree path has five edges,
although A-C is a direct edge. Backtracking means returning to a previous call
or stack frame to inspect another branch. These notes are synthetic.

resources.title: Weighted paths
resources.text:
Synthetic notes. In a directed graph with nonnegative weights, path cost is the sum of its edge weights. Edges are S→A (2), S→B (5), A→B (1), A→T (6), B→T (2). Minimum cost from S to T is 5 along S–A–B–T. The two-edge path S–A–T costs 8. Dijkstra settles the vertex with smallest tentative distance. The settled order is S (0), A (2), B (3), T (5). Relax u→v by setting d(v) to the minimum of its current value and d(u)+w(u,v). Nonnegative edge weights justify settling a distance. BFS minimizes edge count and need not minimize arbitrary weighted cost.
The settling proof uses the first unsettled vertex Y on a hypothetical cheaper path to X. Its settled predecessor has relaxed to Y, and d(X)≤d(Y)≤prefix cost≤whole path cost when remaining weights are nonnegative. A counterexample without that assumption has only S→A(1), S→B(2), B→A(-3): the shortest cost to A is -1 even though A can be selected at 1 before B. These derivations are authored synthetic notes, not official solutions.

resources.title: Conditional probability
resources.text: Synthetic notes. Conditional probability P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E), provided P(E)>0. Suppose 20% of messages are urgent, an alert catches 80% of urgent messages and flags 10% of other messages. Among 1000 messages: 160 urgent alerts, 40 urgent without alert, 80 nonurgent alerts, 720 nonurgent without alert. Therefore P(urgent|alert)=160/240=2/3. This differs from P(alert|urgent)=0.8. The probability of an alert is 0.8×0.2+0.1×0.8=0.24. For n independent trials with identical success probability p, P(X=k)=binomial(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k) for integer 0≤k≤n. With n=3,p=1/2, probabilities for k=0,1,2,3 are 1/8,3/8,3/8,1/8. Expected count is the sum of kP(X=k)=np=1.5. A change in independence or p invalidates that binomial model.
